title: Your Impact on Others
keyIdea: Intent is what you meant to do. Impact is how your words or actions actually felt to the other person. They are not always the same: a joke you meant to be funny can still hurt. Read the clues in someone's face, body and words to see the impact. Before you act, predict how it will land. If you are not sure, check in and ask. After a problem, think about what you could do differently next time.

kid: When you do or say something, there are two sides. Your intent is what you meant. The impact is how it felt to the other person. You can mean well and still hurt someone, like laughing when a friend trips.

You cannot see inside someone's head, but you can look for clues. A face that goes red, someone going quiet, or a person walking away are clues that it landed badly. A smile, a laugh with you, or lots of questions are clues it landed well.
Your own feelings are not the clue. If you were laughing, that tells you how you felt, not how they felt. Watch them, not yourself.

Stop and think before you act. Ask yourself: how will this feel for them? If you are not sure afterwards, check in: 'Was that okay?' Then listen. Saying 'I didn't mean it' does not undo the impact, but asking and fixing it can help.
adult: This lesson teaches the gap between intent and impact. Intent is what a child meant. Impact is the effect the action really had on someone else. It sits in the social and emotional learning strands that CASEL calls self-awareness, social awareness and responsible decision-making. That last one includes thinking ahead about the consequences of your actions. In England it supports the statutory Relationships Education guidance (DfE, 2019) on caring friendships and respectful relationships. It also matches the PSHE Association Key Stage 2 aim of learning how words and actions affect others.

Key words for ages 8 to 9: intent, impact, consequence, perspective, empathy, and cues such as facial expression, body language and tone of voice. Children also learn to predict, reflect and check in. The skill has three parts. First, read the impact from cues after the event. Second, predict the impact before acting. Third, after a conflict, reflect on what you could have done differently.

Common mistakes: judging an action only by its intent ('I was only joking', so no harm was done). Reading your own feelings as theirs ('I was laughing, so it was fine'). Telling someone how they feel ('You're fine, right?') instead of asking. Blaming the other person for being hurt ('You're too sensitive'). Acting first and explaining later. A simple family routine helps: stop, predict, then check in.

In the lab your child drags a dot along an impact meter to show how an action landed, using a clue. Next they drag the real clue into a box, not the intent or a detail that tells you nothing. Then they test choices on the meter before acting. They rewind a story and replay a better move. Last, they pick a check-in that asks instead of tells. Every drag has a button twin.

familyTip: When your child says 'I didn't mean it', agree first: 'I know you didn't.' Then ask: 'How do you think it felt for them? What clue tells you?' Model it yourself when you get something wrong: 'I meant to help, but I think I made you feel rushed.'

visual.caption: Intent or impact? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: impact: how it felt to them

lab.caption: Flagship lab: read impact on a meter from clues, find the real clue, test choices before acting, rewind a story, check in.

practice.prompt: Zara says, "Your hair looks funny today!" She meant it as a joke. Lucy looks down and goes quiet. What was the impact?
choices: There was no impact because it was a joke
practice.hint: Look at what Lucy did, not at what Zara meant.
practice.explain: Looking down and going quiet are clues that Lucy felt hurt. The intent was a joke, but the impact was hurt.

practice.prompt: At break you tell {n} friends that only you and one friend can play your game. Everyone else is left out. How many friends are left out?
practice.hint: One friend gets to play. Take that one away from {n}.
practice.explain: {n} friends take away the 1 who plays leaves {=n-1} left out. One choice can have an impact on lots of people at once.

practice.prompt: You are not sure if your joke upset Tom. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Tell the joke again to check
practice.hint: Which choice lets Tom tell you how he feels?
practice.explain: Asking and listening lets Tom tell you the impact. Saying 'You're fine' tells him how to feel instead of finding out.

practice.prompt: You borrow a pencil and keep it for {n} lessons. Your friend needs it in every lesson. In how many lessons did your friend go without it?
practice.hint: Your friend misses the pencil in every lesson you keep it.
practice.explain: Your friend went without it for {n} lessons. You may have meant to give it back, but the impact grew each lesson.

pool.prompt: What is the difference between intent and impact?
choices: Intent is what you meant; impact is how it felt to them
Impact is what you meant; intent is how they felt
pool.hint: Think: which one is inside your head, and which one happens to the other person?
pool.explain: Intent is what you meant to do. Impact is how it actually felt to the other person. They can be different.

pool.prompt: Which is a clue about how someone feels?
choices: Their face goes red and they look away
pool.hint: Clues come from the other person's face, body and words.
pool.explain: A red face and looking away are body-language clues. Your own thoughts are your intent, and a jumper tells you nothing about feelings.

pool.prompt: Before you take the last slice of pizza, what should you do?
choices: Think about how the others will feel, then ask
Take it quickly before anyone sees
Take it, because you were hungriest
pool.hint: This is about predicting the impact before you act.
pool.explain: Predicting how others will feel, then asking, stops an unfair impact before it happens.

pool.prompt: Your friend says, "That really hurt my feelings." What is the best reply?
choices: "I didn't know. I'm sorry it hurt."
pool.hint: Which reply listens to the impact instead of arguing about intent?
pool.explain: Saying sorry for the hurt accepts the impact. 'Only joking' talks about your intent, and 'too sensitive' blames your friend.

pool.prompt: Kai was telling you about his trip. You cut in to talk about yours, and he went quiet. Next time, what could you do differently?
choices: Listen, then ask him a question about his trip
Talk louder so he hears you
pool.hint: Think about what would make Kai feel heard.
pool.explain: Listening and asking a question shows Kai you care about his story. That is reflecting on what you could do differently.

pool.prompt: Ben laughs when he sees his friend fall over. He thinks, "It looked so funny." Which word describes Ben's thought?
pool.hint: Is it what Ben meant, or what happened to his friend?
pool.explain: 'It looked funny' is Ben's intent. The impact is how his friend felt, perhaps hurt or embarrassed.

pool.prompt: You shout "Rubbish team!" at the {n} players who lost. How many players could feel the impact of your words?
pool.hint: Your words were aimed at the whole team. Count every player.
pool.explain: All {n} players heard it, so all {n} could feel hurt. Words aimed at a group can have an impact on everyone in it.

pool.prompt: {n} children are waiting for the swing. You stay on and never give a turn. How many children miss out?
pool.hint: Everyone who is waiting misses out if you never take turns.
pool.explain: All {n} children miss out. Taking turns changes the impact for every one of them.

pool.prompt: Why is "I didn't mean it" not enough on its own?
choices: It talks about your intent, but the other person still felt the impact
Because saying sorry is never needed
pool.hint: Think about who still feels the hurt after you explain.
pool.explain: Explaining your intent can help, but the other person still felt the impact. Asking how they feel and putting it right matters too.
